reviews.question: A non-flow reversible process takes place according to V = 15/P m³, where P is in bar. What will be the work done if pressure changes from 1 bar to 10 bar? [Given ln(10) = 2.3025.]

The process is PV = 15 bar·m³. Hence V₁ = 15 m³ and V₂ = 1.5 m³ as pressure rises from 1 to 10 bar.
P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ and V₁/V₂ = P₂/P₁ = 10.
For the reversible non-flow process, work by the gas is
W = ∫[V₁→V₂] P dV = 15∫[15→1.5] dV/V
  = 15 ln(V₂/V₁) bar·m³
  = −15 ln 10 × 10⁵ J
  = −34.5375 × 10⁵ J = −3.45375 MN·m.
The negative sign indicates compression: work input is 3.4538 MN·m, matching (c).

Given V = 15/P m³, P₁ = 1 bar and P₂ = 10 bar.
P₁V₁ = P₂V₂.
P₁/P₂ = V₂/V₁; V₁/V₂ = 10/1.
Non-flow work = ∫ P dV = ∫[10→1] (15/V) dV
= 15∫[10→1] (1/V) dV
= 15[ln 1 − ln 10]
= 15[0 − 2.3025]
= −34.538 × 10⁵ N·m
= −3.4538 MN·m
= 3.4538 MN·m (compression).

reviews.question: Specific heat at constant pressure can be given as (where γ is the ratio of specific heats at constant pressure and constant volume, R is a gas constant, and J is the Joule constant):

Cₚ − Cₚ/γ = R/J.
Cₚ(γ − 1)/γ = R/J.

Cₚ − Cₚ/γ = R/J.
Cₚ(γ − 1)/γ = R/J.
Cₚ = [γ·R/(γ − 1)]/J = γR/[J(γ − 1)].

reviews.question:
Which of the following are intensive properties?
(1) Density; (2) Pressure; (3) Energy; (4) Enthalpy; (5) Temperature.
reviews.explanation:
Intensive properties do not depend on the amount of a homogeneous system. Density, pressure and temperature are intensive: items 1, 2 and 5, (b). Energy and enthalpy without the word “specific” denote total quantities and are extensive.
Examples of intensive properties include pressure, temperature, density, thermal conductivity and specific energies. Examples of extensive properties include volume, mass, kinetic energy, potential energy, enthalpy, entropy and internal energy.
Density ρ = mass/volume is intensive because both numerator and denominator scale with system size. Specific enthalpy, specific entropy and specific internal energy are also intensive, as is specific volume. Heat capacity is extensive; specific heat capacity is intensive. A ratio of extensive properties is size-independent when both scale with the same system size. The source’s exception for “specific density” is not a valid general rule.
reviews.sourceExplanation:
Intensive Properties: Properties independent of mass are known as intensive properties. Examples: pressure, temperature, density, thermal conductivity and all specific energy, etc.
Extensive Properties: Properties which depend upon the mass of the system are known as extensive properties. Examples: volume, mass, all forms of energy [K.E., P.E., enthalpy, entropy and internal energy], etc.
Note:
1. The ratio of two extensive properties are known as intensive properties. Density (ρ) = mass (extensive)/volume (extensive) → intensive.
2. All specific forms except specific density are always intensive properties. Examples: specific enthalpy, specific entropy, specific internal energy, etc.
• Heat capacity is an extensive property.

reviews.explanation:
Under the usual simple-compressible models, all three have zero relevant work, (d):
• Constant-volume boundary work: V = constant, dV = 0, so Wb = ∫P dV = 0.
• Free expansion: the opposing pressure is zero, hence W = ∫Pext dV = 0. If the enclosing container is insulated, Q = 0 as well; an ideal gas then has equal initial and final temperatures. • Standard throttling: there is no shaft or moving-boundary work and it is usually adiabatic. Neglecting changes in kinetic and potential energy, the steady-flow first law gives h₁ = h₂ = constant; the process is isenthalpic.
Electrical or other work can occur at fixed volume, so the first statement refers to displacement work, and throttling flow work is included in enthalpy.

At constant volume: V = constant, dV = 0. Work done W = P dV = P × 0 = 0.
Free expansion: W = 0, Q = 0. In the free expansion of an ideal gas, even though initial and final temperatures are same, the process is not isothermal because temperature reduces in between.
Throttling process: no change in enthalpy from one state to another state (h₁ = h₂ = h = constant). No work done (W = 0). Process is adiabatic (Q = 0). Process called isenthalpic.

reviews.question: The temperature in a process in which work is done by expanding a gas under adiabatic condition will

options.d: Decrease/increase depending on properties of gas

reviews.explanation:
For the intended ideal-gas closed-system process, neglecting changes in kinetic and potential energy, the first law is Q₁₂ = ΔU₁₂ + W₁₂. Adiabatic means Q₁₂ = 0. If the gas does positive work W₁₂ > 0, then ΔU₁₂ = −W₁₂ < 0. Since ΔU = mCᵥ(T₂ − T₁), T₂ < T₁: temperature decreases, (b). For a reversible path, mCᵥdT = −P dV and dT = −P dV/(mCᵥ) < 0 during expansion.
The printed diagram instead shows gas separated from vacuum by a removable barrier. That is free expansion, which does no work and leaves ideal-gas temperature unchanged; it does not illustrate the question’s specified work-producing expansion. The source also uses Cₚ and an extraneous pressure factor in its algebra; the derivation here uses Cᵥ correctly.
reviews.sourceExplanation:
For expansion of gas under adiabatic condition. The sketch has gas on the left, vacuum on the right, and a barrier between them.
Let process 1–2 be adiabatic expansion of ideal gas, Q₁₂ = 0.
We know Q₁₂ = U₁₂ + W₁₂.
−U₁₂ = W₁₂ ⇒ −mCₚdT = ∫[1→2]P dV.
dT = −[P/(mCₚ)]∫[1→2]P dV ⇒ dT < 0.
So temperature will decrease during the adiabatic expansion.

reviews.question: Which of the following is an example of irreversible process?
reviews.explanation:
Unrestricted expansion of a gas is intrinsically irreversible because it takes place across a finite pressure difference and cannot be reversed without a net environmental change; (b) is the definite example. A polytropic or isothermal path can be reversible when carried out quasi-statically without dissipation. Electrolysis can approach a reversible limit with infinitesimal overpotential, although practical cells have losses.
The source lists the main irreversibility mechanisms: mechanical and fluid friction, unrestricted expansion, and heat transfer through a finite temperature difference. Actual processes usually have some irreversibility. Such effects destroy available work, rather than destroy energy or necessarily cause a “loss of heat.”

In actual practice, most processes are irreversible to some degree. The main causes for irreversibility may be: (i) mechanical and fluid friction; (ii) unrestricted expansion; (iii) heat transfer with a finite temperature difference.

reviews.question: An ideal gas is heated from temperature T₁ to T₂ by keeping its volume constant. The gas is expanded back to its initial temperature according to the law PVⁿ = C. If the entropy changes in the two processes are equal, then the value of n in terms of the adiabatic index γ is:
reviews.explanation:
Let r = T₂/T₁ > 1. During constant-volume heating from T₁ to T₂, Δs₁ = Cᵥ ln r. During the following polytropic expansion back to T₁, TVⁿ⁻¹ = constant, so Vfinal/Vheated = r¹⁄⁽ⁿ⁻¹⁾. Its entropy change is
Δs₂ = Cᵥ ln(T₁/T₂) + R ln(Vfinal/Vheated)
    = −Cᵥ ln r + [R/(n − 1)]ln r.
Equating the signed entropy increases Δs₁ = Δs₂ and cancelling ln r gives
2Cᵥ = R/(n − 1).
Since R = Cₚ − Cᵥ, 2(n − 1) = Cₚ/Cᵥ − 1 = γ − 1.
2n − 2 = γ − 1; 2n = γ + 1.
n = (γ + 1)/2, (a).
The source reaches this result but starts with inconsistent volume/temperature ratio labels; the expansion volume ratio is written consistently here.
reviews.sourceExplanation:
Cᵥ ln(T₂/T₁) = Cᵥ ln(T₁/T₂) + R ln(V₁/V₂).
V₁/V₂ = (T₁/T₂)¹⁄⁽ⁿ⁻¹⁾.
Cᵥ ln(T₂/T₁) = Cᵥ ln(T₁/T₂) + [R/(n − 1)]ln(T₂/T₁).
Cᵥ ln(T₂/T₁) = −Cᵥ ln(T₂/T₁) + [R/(n − 1)]ln(T₂/T₁).
2Cᵥ = R/(n − 1).
Cₚ − Cᵥ = R.
2Cᵥ = (Cₚ − Cᵥ)/(n − 1).
2(n − 1) = Cₚ/Cᵥ − 1.
2n − 2 = γ − 1.
2n = γ + 1.
n = (γ + 1)/2.

reviews.question: During a process involving one kg of working fluid in an insulated cylinder-piston arrangement the temperature of the fluid decreases from 350°C to 250°C. = 1 × 0.8 × (350 − 250)
= 1 × 0.8 × 100
= 80 kJ (by the system).

reviews.question: Extensive property of a system is one whose value

options.a: depends on the mass of the system, like volume
options.b: does not depend on the mass of the system like temperature
options.c: is not dependent on the path followed but on the state
options.d: is dependent on the path followed and not on the state

reviews.explanation:
An extensive property scales with the amount or mass of the system, such as volume, so (a). Examples include volume, mass, kinetic and potential energy, enthalpy, entropy and internal energy. (Entropy is extensive but is not a form of energy.)
Intensive properties are independent of the amount: pressure, temperature, density, thermal conductivity and specific energies. Ratios of equally scaling extensive quantities are intensive; density ρ = mass/volume is an example. Specific enthalpy and specific entropy are intensive, and so is specific volume. The source’s vague exception for “specific density” does not establish a general rule. Heat capacity is extensive, whereas specific heat capacity is intensive.
reviews.sourceExplanation:
Extensive properties—The property which depends upon the mass of the system is known as an extensive property. Examples—volume, mass, all forms of energy (K.E., P.E., enthalpy, entropy and internal energy).
Intensive properties—The property independent of mass is known as an intensive property. Examples—pressure, temperature, density, thermal conductivity, etc., and all specific energy.
Note:
(1) The ratio of two extensive properties is known as an intensive property. Density (ρ) = mass (extensive)/volume (extensive); density is intensive.
(2) All specific forms except specific density are always intensive properties. Examples—specific enthalpy, specific entropy, etc.
(3) Heat capacity is an extensive property.

reviews.question: When air expands from initial pressure P₁ and volume V₁ to final volume 5V₁ following the law PVⁿ = C:

options.a: greater the value of n, greater the work obtained
options.b: smaller the value of n, smaller the work obtained
options.c: for n= 0, the work obtained is the greatest
options.d: forn= 1.4, the work obtained is the greatest

reviews.explanation:
For a quasi-static expansion from the same P₁,V₁ to 5V₁,
W(n) = ∫[V₁→5V₁]P₁(V₁/V)ⁿdV
     = P₁V₁∫[1→5]x⁻ⁿdx.
For every x > 1, x⁻ⁿ decreases as n increases; therefore work strictly decreases with increasing n. For n ≠ 1, W = (P₁V₁ − P₂V₂)/(n − 1); for n = 1, W = P₁V₁ln 5. This confirms the source’s relative-curve argument.
If n is restricted to nonnegative values, n = 0 (constant pressure) gives the greatest work, W = 4P₁V₁, which is the intended key (c). The question supplies no such restriction. Negative indices are valid polytropic paths and yield still larger work: for n = −1, W = 12P₁V₁. There is no greatest work over unrestricted n. Thus (c) is not unconditionally true, while (a), (b) and (d) are also false as general comparisons; no unique unqualified option is justified.
reviews.sourceExplanation:
Given air expands: initial pressure P₁, initial volume V₁, final volume 5V₁; PVⁿ = C. For expansion, the P–V sketch shows three falling curves n₁, n₂, n₃ from P₁,V₁ to V₂, with n₁ < n₂ < n₃. Larger the value of n, smaller is work obtained.
W = (P₁V₁ − P₂V₂)/(n − 1) → “Isotropic process”.
For n = 0 [P = constant], the work obtained is greatest.
reviews.note: Source intended (c) silently assumes nonnegative n. The native stem gives no range; a direct n = −1 counterexample disproves the claimed unrestricted maximum. Original curve reasoning and formula retained.

reviews.question: Which law states that change of internal energy of a perfect gas is directly proportional to the change of temperature.
reviews.explanation:
Joule’s law says the internal energy of a fixed amount of ideal/perfect gas is a function of temperature alone. For constant Cᵥ, ΔU = mCᵥΔT, giving the stated proportionality, (d).
For comparison: Boyle’s law gives V ∝ 1/P for fixed mass and temperature (the source omits “inversely”); Charles’s law gives V ∝ T at fixed mass and pressure; Gay-Lussac’s law gives P ∝ T at fixed mass and volume. The last two require absolute temperature. More generally for an ideal gas, ΔU = m∫Cᵥ(T)dT, so exact linear proportionality assumes constant heat capacity.
reviews.sourceExplanation:
Boyle’s law—The volume of a given mass of a gas varies as its absolute pressure, provided the moles and temperature remain constant.
Charles’s law—The volume of a given gas varies directly as its absolute temperature provided the moles and pressure are kept constant.
Gay-Lussac’s law—The pressure of a given mass of a gas varies directly as its absolute temperature provided the moles and volume are kept constant.
Joule’s law—This law states that the internal energy of a given quantity of a gas depends on the temperature.

reviews.question: Consider the following statements about thermodynamic properties of system : 1. Heat transferred at constant volume increase the internal energy of the system. 2. Heat transferred at constant pressure increases the enthalpy of a system. 3. The enthalpy of an ideal gas depends on the temperature only. Which of these statements are correct?
reviews.explanation:
Under the standard closed simple-compressible assumptions with only displacement work, all three statements hold, (a).
1. At constant volume, W = ∫P dV = 0, so heat added gives Qᵥ = ΔU.
2. At constant pressure, Qₚ = ΔU + PΔV = Δ(U + PV) = ΔH.
3. For an ideal gas of fixed composition, h = h(T), so enthalpy depends only on temperature.
The first two results require no electrical, shaft or other non-PV work and negligible kinetic and potential energy changes; the third is the ideal-gas property relation.

reviews.question: Consider the following properties : 1. Specific heat 2. Thermal diffusivity 3. Dynamic viscosity 4. Density Which of these properties of air increase with increase of temperature ?
reviews.explanation:
For ordinary air over engineering temperature ranges at approximately fixed pressure, specific heat, thermal diffusivity and dynamic viscosity increase with temperature, while density decreases. Thus items 1, 2 and 3 are intended, (d).
The ideal-gas density relation is PV = mRT ⇒ P = (m/V)RT = ρRT ⇒ P/ρ = RT. At fixed pressure, ρ = P/(RT) and T ∝ 1/ρ.
Thermal diffusivity is α = k/(ρCₚ); its temperature behavior follows from the temperature-dependent transport properties and density. These increases are trends, not exact direct proportionalities to T, as the source suggests. The fixed-pressure condition matters for the density comparison.

The properties of air increase with increase of temperature such as:
PV = mRT ⇒ P = (m/V)RT ⇒ P = ρRT.
P/ρ = RT ⇒ T ∝ 1/ρ.
T is inversely proportional to density ρ.
• T is directly proportional to specific heat, thermal diffusivity and dynamic viscosity.

reviews.question: When 2 gm of a gas A is introduced into an evacuated flask kept at 25°C, the pressure is found to be 1 atmosphere. If 3 gm of another gas B is then added to the same flask, the total pressure becomes 1.5 atmospheres. Assuming ideal gas behaviour, the ratio of molecular weights, M, : Mg will be
reviews.explanation:
At the same flask volume and temperature, each ideal-gas partial pressure satisfies PiV = (mi/Mi)RᵤT. Initially PA = 1 atm; after adding gas B, total pressure is 1.5 atm, so PB = 1.5 − 1 = 0.5 atm.
MA = mARᵤT/(PAV) = 2RᵤT/V.
MB = mBRᵤT/(PBV) = 3RᵤT/(0.5V).
MA/MB = [2RᵤT/V][0.5V/(3RᵤT)] = 1/3.
Therefore MA:MB = 1:3, (a).
reviews.sourceExplanation:
Given WA = 2 gm, WB = 3 gm, PA = 1 atm, Ptotal = 1.5 atm.
Ideal gas equation PV = nRT.
n = W (Weight of tubes)/M (Molecular weight).
PV = (W/M)RT. M = WRT/(PV).
MA = W₁RT/(P₁V) = 2RT/(1 × V). [Pt = 1.5 atm and Pt = PA + PB.]
MB = W₂RT/(P₂V) = 3RT/(0.5V).
MA/MB = (2RT/V) × (0.5V/3RT) = 1:3.

reviews.question:
Consider the following statements about heat and work:
1. Both are path functions.
2. Both are exact differentials.
3. Work is low-grade energy and heat is high-grade energy.
4. Heat is low-grade energy and work is high-grade energy.
Which of the following options are true?
reviews.explanation: Heat and work depend on the path and have inexact differentials δQ and δW, so Statement 1 is true and Statement 2 false. Work can be completely dissipated into heat, while conversion of heat into work in a cycle is constrained by the second law. In the conventional availability terminology, work is high-grade energy and heat is lower-grade energy, so Statement 4 is true and Statement 3 false. The correct combination is 1 and 4, (c). Heat’s available work fraction depends on the heat-source temperature relative to the environment.

2. Heat is low-grade energy and work is high-grade energy.

reviews.question: An adiabatic process is one in which :

options.a: no heat enters or leaves the gas
options.b: the change in internal energy is equal to work done
options.c: the temperature of the gas changes

reviews.explanation: The defining statement is that no heat enters or leaves the gas, Q = 0: (a). For a closed system with negligible kinetic and potential energy changes, δQ = dU + δWby gives 0 = dU + δWby, or δWby = −dU. Thus internal-energy change equals work done on the gas and is the negative of work done by it; choice (b) omits that sign/direction distinction. Temperature need not change: an insulated ideal-gas free expansion has Q = W = 0 and ΔT = 0. Consequently (c) is not a necessary property and “all of the above” (d) is false.
reviews.sourceExplanation:
Adiabatic Process—
• No heat enters or leaves the gas.
• The change in internal energy is equal to work done.
δQ = dU + δW.
0 = dU + δW.
δW = −dU.
• The temperature of the gas changes.
reviews.note: Corrected printed key (d) to the defining condition (a). The full source first-law steps and its unjustified temperature assertion are retained.

reviews.question: The coefficient of linear expansion of a solid is L. The volume V of a cube of this solid on being heated by 1°C will change by
reviews.explanation:
Let cube side be a, so V = a³. Taking logarithms, log V = log a³ = 3 log a. Differentiating gives dV/V = 3 da/a. Linear expansion coefficient L implies da/a = LΔT. For ΔT = 1°C,
dV = 3(da/a)V = 3(L × 1)V = 3VL, (b).
This is the first-order small-expansion result; the exact finite change is V[(1 + L)³ − 1] when L is treated as constant over that one-degree interval.

Coefficient of linear expansion of a solid = L. Volume = V, ΔT = 1°C.
V = a³.
Take log both sides: log V = log a³ = 3 log a.
Partially differentiate both sides: dV/V = 3 da/a.
dV = 3(da/a)V
= 3(L × 1)V
= 3VL.

reviews.question: A well insulated vessel containing air is heated to double the pressure and temperature 150% in excess of initial, The amount of air that leaked is
reviews.explanation:
For a fixed-volume vessel containing ideal air, m = PV/(RT), even if some mass leaks. The final pressure is P₂ = 2P₁. A temperature “150% in excess of initial” means T₂ = T₁ + 1.5T₁ = 2.5T₁, with temperature ratios in kelvins. Therefore

Fraction leaked = 1 − 0.8 = 0.20 = 20%, (a).
The source instead substitutes 1.5T₁ (which means only 50% above initial), varies V rather than gas mass, and obtains 25%. That does not solve the given leaky fixed-vessel problem. If T₂ really were 1.5T₁, a fixed-volume pressure doubling would require mass gain, not leakage.

For ideal gas P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂ (air is an ideal gas).
P₁V₁/T₁ = 2P₁V₂/(1.5T₁).
V₁ = (4/3)V₂.
The amount of air leaked = (V₁ − V₂)/V₁ %
= [V₁ − (3/4)V₁]/V₁ %
= 25%.

reviews.question: The specific heat of a diatomic gas at constant pressure is given by (R = universal gas constant and M = molecular weight of gas):
reviews.explanation:
For the ordinary rigid diatomic ideal-gas model with rotational modes active and vibrational modes frozen, f = 5. Therefore Cᵥ,molar = 5R/2, Cₚ,molar = Cᵥ,molar + R = 7R/2 and γ = 7/5 = 1.4. Per unit mass, the gas constant is Rg = R/M, so
cₚ = γRg/(γ − 1)
   = 1.4Rg/(1.4 − 1) = 1.4Rg/0.4
   = 1.4R/(0.4M) = 7R/(2M), (c).
R is the universal gas constant, Rg the characteristic/specific gas constant and M molecular weight. In the same equipartition framework γ = 1 + 2/f; a monatomic gas has f = 3 and γ = 5/3 ≈ 1.67, while a diatomic gas has f = 5. The source states a minimum γ = 1 and maximum 1.67; γ approaches 1 as the number of active modes becomes large, rather than attaining 1 for finite f. Diatomic heat capacities change outside the assumed temperature range.
reviews.sourceExplanation:
We know cₚ = γRg/(γ − 1). For diatomic γ = 7/5 = 1.4. Rg = R/M.
cₚ = γRg/(γ − 1) = 1.4Rg/(1.4 − 1)
= 1.4Rg/0.4 = 1.4R/(0.4M) [Rg = R/M].
cₚ = 7R/(2M).
R = universal gas constant; Rg = characteristic gas constant; M = molecular weight.
For monoatomic γ = 5/3 = 1.66; the minimum value of γ = 1 and maximum is 1.67. The general formula for γ of any gas is γ = 1 + 2/f, where f = degree of freedom, for monoatomic f = 3 and for diatomic f = 5.

reviews.question:
A 100 W electric bulb was switched on in a 2.5 m × 3 m × 3 m thermally insulated room having temperature 20°C. The room temperature at the end of 24 h will be:
Consider density and specific heat of air as 1.2 kg/cm³ and 0.718 kW/°C/kg [units as printed].
reviews.explanation:
The source intends a rigid insulated room with only its air absorbing the bulb’s electrical input, density 1.2 kg/m³ and Cᵥ = 0.718 kJ/(kg·K). With those intended coherent units:
Electrical input = 100 W × (24 × 60 × 60) s = 8.64 × 10⁶ J = 8640 kJ.
Air mass m = ρV = 1.2 × 2.5 × 3 × 3 = 27 kg.
The room is insulated, so electrical work input raises the internal energy of the air:
8640 = 27 × 0.718(T₂ − 20).
T₂ = 20 + 8640/(27 × 0.718) ≈ 465.68°C, nearest the supplied 470°C, (b).
However, the native stem actually prints density in kg/cm³ and the specific-heat unit as kW/°C/kg. The first gives a billion-fold different air mass, and kW/(kg·°C) is not a specific-heat unit. The literal given quantities cannot support this calculation or a unique valid option. The source key (b) is retained, but this item is not auto-graded until its givens are corrected.

Heat supply to thermally insulated room:
Q = 100 × 24 × 60 × 60 = 8640 kJ.
Mass of air in room m = ρair × volume of room
= 1.2 × 2.5 × 3 × 3.
m = 27 kg.
Heat supply to insulated room = rise in internal energy of air inside the room.
8640 = 27 × 0.718(T₂ − 20°).
T₂ = 465°C ≈ 470°C.

reviews.question: 170 kJ of heat is supplied to a system at constant volume. Then the system rejects 180 kJ of heat at constant pressure and 40 kJ of work is done on it. The system is finally brought to its original state by an adiabatic process. If the initial value of internal energy is 100 kJ, then which one of the following statements is correct?

options.a: the highest value of internal energy occurs at the end of the constant volume process
options.b: the highest value of internal energy occurs at the end of the constant pressure process
options.c: the highest value of internal energy occurs after adiabatic expansion
options.d: internal energy is equal at all the points.

reviews.explanation:
Label the initial state 1, the end of constant-volume heating 2, and the end of constant-pressure cooling 3. Given U₁ = 100 kJ.
1 → 2, constant volume: W₁₂ = 0 and Q₁₂ = +170 kJ. From Q = ΔU + W,
170 = U₂ − U₁ + 0, so U₂ = 170 + 100 = 270 kJ.
2 → 3, constant pressure: Q₂₃ = −180 kJ, while 40 kJ work is done on the system, so W₂₃,by = −40 kJ.
−180 = U₃ − U₂ − 40.
U₃ = U₂ − 140 = 130 kJ.
3 → 1 is adiabatic: Q₃₁ = 0 and U₁ − U₃ = −30 kJ, so W₃₁,by = 30 kJ.
Thus U₂ > U₃ > U₁, namely 270 > 130 > 100 kJ. The highest endpoint internal energy is at the end of the constant-volume process, (a). The cycle sketch shows vertical heating 1–2, horizontal compression 2–3, and curved adiabatic expansion 3–1.
reviews.sourceExplanation:
Diagram: P–V cycle with 1 at lower right, 2 at upper right and 3 at upper left. Q₂ = 180 kJ is directed out of process 2–3; Q₁ = 170 kJ is directed into process 1–2.
1 → 2 constant volume. 2 → 3 constant pressure. 3 → 1 adiabatic.
U₁ = 100 kJ; Q₂ = 180 kJ; Q₁ = 170 kJ.
In process 1 → 2:
δQ = dU + δW.
170 = dU + 0.
170 = U₂ − U₁.
U₂ = 170 + U₁.
U₂ = 170 + 100 = 270 kJ.
In process 2–3:
δQ = dU + δW.
−180 = U₃ − U₂ − 40.
U₃ = 130 kJ.
Highest value of internal energy occurs at end of constant-volume process, U₂ = 270.
